t.aktash@50.3,87.6:
Aktash is a small village on the Chuya Highway, the road that runs from Novosibirsk through the Altai mountains toward the Mongolian border and is often named by Russian riders as the finest motorcycle road in the country. The name means white stone in the Turkic languages of the area, and the village sits where the Chuya river runs out of a deep valley between peaks that wear snow from autumn into early summer. About three thousand people live here, enough to keep a shop, a small café or two and a petrol station going.

The surroundings are the attraction. The Chuya Highway follows the river upward through gorges, then across the open Kurai steppe farther on, while the high Altai ridges stand off to the south, tipped with ice. The road's surface has been improved over the years, though patches of frost heave and potholes remain, and the bends are the long, open sort that suit a loaded bike well. Cloud, wind and rain can all arrive within an hour. Summer is warm in the valleys but freezing at the top of the passes, and from October frost and snow become a risk.

The history of the road is old. The Chuya Tract was a trade route for caravans heading from Siberia to Mongolia, and tea, silk and furs travelled along it. In the early twentieth century it was widened for carts and later for motor vehicles, and today it carries trucks and tourists to the Mongolian border at Tashanta. Aktash also had a mercury mine and processing in the twentieth century, a reminder that the Altai mountains are rich in minerals. The region holds many ancient burial mounds and rock carvings, including those at Kalbak-Tash, which lie within a short ride and record the passage of nomads over thousands of years.

Treat fuel with care. Stations are spaced out along the valley, but a few have been known to run dry, so fill up whenever you see a pump. Simple guesthouses and cafés serve hot soup, dumplings and tea, and the people are hospitable. Altai honey, sold at roadside stalls, is a good thing to carry in the tank bag.
t.gorno altaysk@52.0,85.9:
Gorno-Altaysk lies where the Altai begins. The capital of the Altai Republic is a small city of about fifty-five thousand people in a green valley at the foot of the mountains, close to the confluence of the Mayma and the Katun, and it is the entry point to a region of snowy peaks, turquoise rivers and big skies. The mountains of the Altai, in the heart of Siberia, are on UNESCO's World Heritage list as the Golden Mountains of Altai, and they reach 4,506 metres at Belukha, the highest peak in Siberia.

From here, the Chuysky Trakt, the M52 highway, runs south-east for hundreds of kilometres, all the way to the Mongolian border. It is often named among the most beautiful roads in the world, and riders will quickly see why. It winds along the Katun River, whose water is a milky turquoise from glacial silt, climbs over passes with long views, and drops into deep valleys with small villages and herds of horses. The surface is good by Russian standards and the bends are smooth, though trucks and tourist buses make some sections busy, and rain, rockfalls or road works can slow the pace.

The Altai is also a landscape of ancient history. The Pazyryk people, nomadic horsemen, buried their chiefs in frozen tombs here more than two thousand years ago, and the ice preserved tattoos, textiles and horses with astonishing detail. The indigenous Altaians keep shamanic traditions, and sacred sites with ribbons tied to trees can be found along the road. Lake Teletskoye, to the north-east, is the deepest lake in the Altai at about 325 metres, and a rough road runs along part of its shore.

Gorno-Altaysk has fuel, food and hotels, and Mayma next door has more. Services along the Chuysky Trakt are regular, but thin out in the far south. The best season is June to September, with cool nights, and snow can arrive early at altitude. Foreign riders should check current rules before planning a trip.
t.manzherok@51.8,85.8:
Manzherok is where the Altai begins to feel like mountains. The village sits on the Katun River, which runs a startling turquoise, colored by glacial silt, through a valley of larch, birch and meadows with snowy peaks beyond. It is the first of a string of resort villages along the Chuysky Trakt, the old highway that runs from Biysk through the Altai Republic to the Mongolian border, and for many riders it is the first moment the road starts to climb in earnest.

The Chuysky Trakt, M52, has a reputation as one of the most beautiful roads in Russia, even in the world, a claim made by travel writers for decades. It follows an ancient caravan route that Russian engineers turned into a proper road in the 1920s and 1930s, and it passes through steppe, taiga and alpine country in the space of a few hundred kilometers. Here at Manzherok, the surroundings are gentle: a small lake, a ski slope with a chairlift that runs in summer for the view, and holiday camps tucked into the trees. Gorno-Altaysk, the republic's capital, is about eighteen kilometers away.

The ride beyond is where the character emerges. The road follows the Katun upstream through green gorges, with the river flashing below, and then climbs through the Seminsky Pass before descending toward Onguday. Surfaces are generally good, but trucks and tour buses make passing awkward, and cattle sometimes graze beside the road. Weather changes quickly in the mountains: bright sunshine can give way to sudden rain, and mountain mist can hide the peaks.

The village has shops, cafes and some fuel along the main road, but Gorno-Altaysk has the bigger stations and supermarkets, so fill the tank there before the climb. In summer, horse flies and gadflies are a nuisance, and in September the nights turn cold. The best months are June and early September, when the air is clear and the larches begin to turn gold. Altai honey, sold at roadside stalls, is a local specialty, and a jar makes a good souvenir. Always check the road conditions after heavy rain, as landslides and washouts can close sections.
t.onguday@50.8,86.2:
Onguday sits on the Chuysky Trakt in the central Altai, a village of several thousand people stretched along the road with the Katun River nearby, and it is the main service stop between the Seminsky Pass and the high steppe further south. The Altai people, a Turkic-speaking group with their own traditions of shamanism and, more recently, of a local faith called Burkhanism, are the heart of the population here, and the villages show their culture in carved wooden figures, festival grounds and yurt-style cafes.

The landscape around is a classic Altai mix: forested ridges, wide river valleys and, to the south, snow-capped peaks along the Mongolian frontier. The road runs through open valleys of larch and pine, with cliffs of pale stone. The nearby Seminsky Pass, at about 1,717 meters, is a notable high point of the highway, with a long, gently winding climb through spruce forest and a view from the top. South of Onguday, the road climbs again over Chike-Taman, a pass of about 1,295 meters built in the 1960s that offers sweeping views, before dropping toward Aktash.

It is an exciting road to ride, though it needs attention. Hairpins and drops, narrow bridges and long grades are common, and the pavement can show frost cracks and patches. Trucks heading to Mongolia use the road, and tourist buses fill it in July and August, so passing demands patience. Cows, sheep and horses wander onto the road without warning, and the weather can change from sun to snow in an hour, even in summer. A warm layer and waterproofs are always wise.

Onguday has fuel stations, shops, guesthouses and cafes, and it is the last place with a wide choice for a good way south, so fill up here. Local food includes lamb dishes, dumplings, and dairy products, and roadside stands sell honey, nuts and berries. The best time to ride is June to early September, with July the warmest, though the nights are cool. Early autumn brings golden larches, and winter closes many side roads. Always check the forecast, since sudden storms can cause rockfall on mountain sections.
t.oroktoy@51.0,86.2:
The Oroktoy Bridge is one of the most photographed spots on the Chuya Highway, and for good reason. The road crosses the Katun River on a long steel span near the village of Oroktoy, with the water below a startling milky turquoise, tinted by glacial flour carried down from the high mountains, and the green, forested walls of the valley rising on both sides. It is the classic Altai view: a bright, fast river, a ribbon of road, and layer upon layer of blue ridges receding into the haze.

The Chuya Highway, known as the Chuysky Trakt, is the great road of the Altai. It runs for about 950 kilometres from Biysk, on the edge of the Siberian plain, to the Mongolian border, following an old caravan route along which traders carried tea, silk and cattle between Russia and Mongolia. The modern road was built in the 1930s, and it has been called one of the most beautiful roads in the world, a claim you start to believe on this stretch. It climbs through birch and larch forest, along river gorges, over passes, and into the high steppe, and each section has a distinct character.

The Katun, the main river of the Altai, rises from the glaciers of Mount Belukha, at 4,506 metres the highest peak in Siberia, and runs north to join the Biya and form the Ob. The water is cold, fast and clear in the upper valley, and the gravel bars are good places to stop for a rest. The region is part of the Golden Mountains of Altai, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and rich in wildlife, including ibex, argali sheep and snow leopards in the remote high country, though you will see none of these from the road.

For riders, the Chuya Highway is a gem, with smooth tarmac, wide curves, and long views, and it is popular with motorcyclists in the summer months. The road is generally well maintained, though frost heave and patches occur, and rockfalls are possible. Traffic includes tourist buses, trucks and cars, and it can be heavy at weekends. The weather is variable, with sun, rain and wind, and temperatures drop quickly at altitude. The best months are June to September, and September, with golden larches, is especially lovely.

Onguday, about twenty-seven kilometres away, has petrol stations and shops. Villages along the road have small shops and cafés, but fuel can be sparse, so fill up whenever you can. Pull over at the bridge, and let the turquoise water fill your eyes. It is a colour you rarely see in a river.
t.kalbak tash@50.7,86.7:
Kalbak-Tash is a place where the ancient peoples of the Altai left a message, carved into rock. The site, a stretch of dark, polished slabs and boulders on the bank of the Chuya River, near the highway, holds one of the largest collections of petroglyphs in Siberia, with several thousand images covering a span of perhaps six thousand years. The earliest are Bronze Age, showing wild animals, hunters and strange sun-headed figures, and later layers, from the Scythian period and from the early Turkic nomads, include deer with branching antlers, horsemen, mounted archers, and runic inscriptions. Some figures are life-size, and the effect of walking among them, with the river nearby and the hills behind, is of stepping into a very old story.

The rock art of the Altai belongs to a wider tradition across Central Asia, the work of herders and warriors who lived on these steppes, buried their chiefs under stone mounds, and honoured the sun, the sky and the animal world. The deer stones of Mongolia and the carved stones of Tuva are cousins of these images, and archaeologists treat the Altai as one of the great cultural crossroads of the ancient world. The nearby Pazyryk burials, in the high valleys, held frozen tombs with preserved textiles, tattooed bodies and horses, a find that astonished the world.

Please respect the site. The carvings are fragile, and climbing on the rocks, touching the images or scratching new marks does lasting damage. Many are better seen in raking light, in the early morning or evening, and a little patience helps you find them.

The Chuya Highway, which passes nearby, is one of the finest roads in Russia for riders. Smooth surface, long bends, wide valleys, the blue of the river alongside, and mountains ahead, all combine in a ride that gets better the further you go. The surface is generally well kept, with some frost heave, and traffic is usually moderate, though tourist buses and trucks appear. In summer, the weather is changeable, and afternoon thunderstorms are common. Dust can be an issue on gravel side roads. The best months are June to September.

Inya, about twenty-four kilometres away, is a small village with basic shops and fuel is not guaranteed, so fill up in Onguday or Gorno-Altaysk. Cafés on the highway offer hot meals, mostly in summer, but the choice is limited. Carry water, a repair kit and warm clothes, because the Altai weather can change very quickly. Stand among the carvings in the late light, and look at the faces of the animals. They have been waiting a long time.
t.chagan uzun@50.1,88.4:
The Chuya Steppe is a surprise after the green valleys of the northern Altai. Beyond the mountain passes, the road drops to a broad, high, open basin of stony plain, with short, dry grass, long views and a big, hard sky, and the mountains stand back on every horizon. It is a cold desert at around 1,700 metres, ringed by snow ranges, a landscape closer to Mongolia than to the Siberian taiga, and Chagan-Uzun lies on its edge, a small settlement near the Chuya River, in the district of Kosh-Agach.

The district has some of the coldest winters in southern Siberia, with temperatures that can drop below minus forty, and the summers are short, dry and sunny, with big swings between day and night. The people are mostly Altaians and Kazakhs, herders who keep sheep, goats, yaks and horses on the steppe, living in wooden houses and yurts, and the local cuisine includes boiled mutton, dairy products and strong tea. The mountains to the south hold the glaciers of the Tavan Bogd range, on the border with Mongolia, and the area is a gateway to high-altitude treks and climbing trips.

The geology tells a violent story. About fourteen thousand years ago, an ice dam in the Chuya basin burst, releasing a flood of glacial meltwater that raced down the Katun valley, leaving giant ripple marks and boulders as big as houses. Geologists count it as one of the largest known floods, and its traces are visible in the landscape, in terraces and gravel bars, along the road.

For a rider, the Chuya Steppe is open, fast and windy. The road runs straight for long stretches, with only the odd curve, and the wind can be savage, pushing a bike sideways, so grip the bars and lean into it. The surface is usually smooth, though frost cracks appear, and trucks heading for the Mongolian border are common. The sun is intense at altitude, and temperatures drop rapidly after dark, so carry warm clothing. Summer is the only comfortable season, from June to early September, and a frost can come at any time.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Services are sparse between settlements, and the nearest border post is a restricted zone, so carry your documents. Climb up the nearest low rise, and look across the plain. The sense of space is complete, and the sky is enormous.
t.ulagan pass@50.5,87.7:
The Ulagan Pass is a high crossing in the heart of the Altai, where the road leaves the Chuya Highway and climbs into a country of rolling, treeless, wind-scoured uplands. It runs between the Chuya valley and the lands around the village of Ust-Ulagan, over a ridge that carries the landscape from forest to tundra, and the summit region, with its big skies, lichen-covered rocks and stunted larch, has an Arctic feel despite the latitude. Clouds drift low across the ridge, and on clear days you can see snow peaks on the horizon, with the long, grey line of the Chulyshman plateau beyond.

The road is part of a network that has become popular with off-road riders and drivers, and the pass is the start of some of the most challenging tracks in the region. In good conditions, the main route is manageable, with gravel and dirt in places, though the surface can be rough, with washouts, rocks and mud. After rain, the clay turns slick, and stream crossings can become deep. A dual-sport bike, good tyres and a sense of caution are the tools you need, and many people travel in groups. Weather changes fast: sun, hail and thick fog can follow each other in an hour, and at altitude, the wind is cold even in July. Snow can fall in any month, and the pass can be closed from late autumn to spring.

The land belongs to the Altaians, a Turkic people with a shamanic tradition and a deep respect for nature. They keep sheep, goats and horses on the high pastures, and you may see herders on horseback, their felt tents and wooden huts dotted along the valleys. Offerings of ribbons are tied to trees at the pass, a custom that marks the place as sacred, and passing travellers often add a coin or a stone. It is considered polite to pause for a moment.

For services, plan carefully. Ust-Ulagan, about twenty-three kilometres away, is a village with small shops and basic supplies, and Aktash, a little farther, has a few more, but fuel is not guaranteed. The sensible approach is to fill up at larger towns on the highway and carry spare, with food, water, repair tools, and warm clothing. Mobile coverage is poor in places.

Stop at the top, take off your helmet, and let the wind settle. The view over the Altai is long and quiet.
t.balykcha@51.3,87.7:
Balykcha lies at the southern end of Lake Teletskoye, the great blue lake of the Altai, and the name has the sound of a place at the end of the road. Teletskoye is about eighty kilometres long, narrow and very deep, with a maximum depth of around 325 metres, and it is held between steep, forested mountains that fall straight into the water. Locals call it the little sister of Baikal, a comparison that is more affectionate than scientific, and the water is clear, cold and drinkable. It is the largest lake in the Altai, and the region around it is part of the Altai Nature Reserve, which is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

The southern shore is wild, forested and roadless, and getting there is part of the challenge. Most visitors reach the lake by road to Artybash at the northern end, and then travel by boat or on foot, since no highway follows the shore. At the south, the Chulyshman River pours into the lake out of a deep gorge, one of the wildest corners of the range, with waterfalls and canyons. The Chulyshman valley is reached by rough tracks, often only passable in dry weather, and is a favourite for jeep expeditions and adventurous riders.

The surrounding forest is cedar, fir, larch and birch, with a rich understory of ferns, berries and mosses, and the air is filled with the scent of resin. Wildlife includes bears, maral deer, sable and a great variety of birds, though you are more likely to hear than see them. The Altaians, who live along the shores and in the valleys, regard the lake as sacred, and local myths speak of giants and spirits.

The tracks in this region are rough, steep and often muddy, with stream crossings and rockfalls, and distances are long, with nothing in between. A dual-sport bike, solid experience and a companion are minimum requirements. The window is short, from late June to September, and weather can turn quickly, with fog and rain sweeping down the lake.

The nearest reliable supplies are a long way off, in towns on the Chuya Highway or at Gorno-Altaysk, so plan your range carefully, carry spare fuel, and bring food, water and a way of making repairs. A boat trip on the lake, from the northern end, is a simpler way of seeing the same scenery. Come in the early morning, when the lake is calm and the mountains are mirrored in the water.
t.altayskoye@52.0,85.3:
Altayskoye is the kind of place a rider passes through without noticing the name, and that is the right way to treat it, with one good reason to stop. It is a large village by any standard, close to fourteen thousand people, set in the green foothills of the northern Altai where the plain begins to crumple into ridges. Belokurikha, the spa town that most visitors are heading for, lies about twenty-four kilometres away, and Starobelokurikha, a much smaller settlement, sits between the two.

Because of its size, this is where you can count on the ordinary comforts: a petrol station or two, shops, cafes serving soup and dumplings, and enough pavement to park a bike and walk for ten minutes. A hamlet in these hills may not offer any of that, so top up here before heading into the mountains. Nothing about the main street is pretty, with low houses, wooden gates and the odd Soviet block, but it has the unhurried feel of an agricultural centre where tractors share the road with the family car.

The riding around it is easy and pleasant rather than dramatic. The surface is mostly decent asphalt with some patched stretches, gradients are mild, and the corners are wide enough to let you look at the scenery, which here means fields of sunflowers and wheat giving way to birch groves and then pine on the higher ground. Summer afternoons bring heat and the occasional thunderstorm rolling off the mountains, so an early start pays off, and the light in September, with the slopes turning yellow, is the best of the year.

If you want a story to carry on with, think of the larger picture. The Altai region here sits where the Siberian plain, the Kazakh steppe and the Mongolian uplands meet, and it has been a crossing place for herders and travellers for thousands of years. The modern settlements are young by comparison, mostly grown from Russian farming colonies in the nineteenth century, and many of the place names still reflect the river and the mountains behind them. Treat Altayskoye as the practical hinge of a loop, buy a bottle of water, eat something warm, and carry on towards the hills with a full tank and a rested back.
t.gorno altaysk@52.0,86.0:
Gorno-Altaysk is the capital of the Altai Republic, a small city of fifty-odd thousand people on the Mayma river, and it sits right where the Siberian plain gives way to mountains. The city itself has a practical look, with Soviet apartment blocks, a long main avenue named for Communism and a modest museum of local history, but it is a place where travellers stock up. It was a trading post called Ulala until the 1930s, and the people of the region, the Altaians, still keep shamanic traditions and the throat-singing epics of their ancestors.

Everything interesting begins just beyond it. The Chuysky Trakt, a road that begins at Biysk and runs southeast toward Mongolia, is among the most famous in Russia, and it follows an old caravan route along the Katun river, a fast, milky-turquoise stream fed by glaciers. The Altai range rises to the south, culminating in Belukha, a double-peaked, snow-covered mountain of about 4,500 metres, the highest in Siberia, regarded as sacred by local peoples. Birch and larch forests cover the lower slopes, meadows are full of wildflowers in June, and the mountains turn gold in September.

The road south of the city is good riding country. Smooth tarmac follows the river in long bends, with views of cliffs, side valleys and bridges over clear streams. The Katun is crossed at several points, and the villages along it have wooden houses and honey for sale at the roadside. Ust-Sema, a short way upriver, is a resort village with the first holiday camps. Weekend traffic from Barnaul and Novosibirsk can be heavy in July and August, with slow lorries and tourist coaches, and mist can drop into the valleys quickly. Cattle and horses sometimes graze on the road.

Gorno-Altaysk has fuel stations and shops, and Mayma, a town of fifteen thousand a few kilometres away, adds more. The road beyond has stations in the larger villages, but the distances increase as you climb toward Mongolia, so top up whenever it is practical. Cafes serve Altai dishes, such as boiled meat with broth, dumplings and a strong tea with milk, and the local honey is excellent.

The best season is June to September, and mornings are cold even then. Expect to see herders, cyclists and a few tourists, and take the time to stop at a viewpoint and listen to the river.
t.ust sema@51.7,85.8:
Ust-Sema is a small village on the Katun river in the Altai Republic, where the river is swift, loud and a startling turquoise. The name means mouth of the Sema, and refers to the smaller river that joins the Katun here. It lies on the Chemal road, a few dozen kilometres south of Gorno-Altaysk, in the foothills of the mountains that form the heart of southern Siberia. The air is fresh and the forest is thick with larch and birch, and behind everything the high peaks stand in layers.

The Katun is the main river of the Altai and starts at a glacier below Belukha, the highest peak in Siberia at 4,506 metres, and the water here is cold and mineral-rich, with a colour that comes from fine glacial silt suspended in it. It runs through a deep, forested valley with rapids, pools and gravel banks, and the sound of it can be heard from the road. The surrounding mountains are part of the Golden Mountains of Altai, a UNESCO World Heritage Site for their rich variety of habitats and the importance of the region in the history of Central Asia.

Chemal, a little way upstream, is the best-known place in this stretch of the valley. A small hydroelectric station sits on the river, and a famous footbridge leads to Patmos, a rocky island in the Katun with a little church on its summit, reached by a swaying suspension bridge. The island is a popular place for visitors, with a view up and down the river. Beyond is the beginning of the true mountain landscape.

The road here follows the river through a series of bends and short climbs, with the Katun alongside, and gives some of the finest riding in southern Siberia, with smooth asphalt in places and rough patches in others. Traffic can be heavy in summer, when visitors from Novosibirsk and Barnaul flood the valley, so go early. Cattle and horses wander across the road in the villages, and watch for rockfall after rain.

Services are modest. Fuel is in Gorno-Altaysk and some larger villages, and it is wise to top up there. In the villages there are small cafés and roadside stalls selling honey, dried fruit and fresh bread, and the local food includes river fish and mutton. The best months are June to September, and autumn colours can be glorious in late September.
t.chike taman pass@50.6,86.3:
Chike-Taman is a mountain pass on the Chuya Highway, the long road that runs from Novosibirsk through the Altai to the Mongolian border, and for many riders it is one of the high points of that journey. It sits at a little under thirteen hundred metres, which is not especially high by alpine standards, but the pass crosses a rugged ridge and offers a sudden change of scenery, with the road dropping from forested slopes into the deep valley of the Katun. On a clear day, the views from the top reach far across layered ranges.

The Chuya Highway, or Chuysky Trakt, is an old route that was a caravan track long before it became a motor road. It was improved in the early twentieth century and is today considered one of the most beautiful roads in the world by those who ride it. It follows the valleys of the Katun and Chuya rivers, passing through mountain gorges, steppe and finally the high plateau near the border. Chike-Taman is one of its signature climbs, with a long run of hairpins and a viewing platform at the top, where local people sell honey, souvenirs and carved wooden objects.

The road up and down is generally in good condition, but it is busy with trucks and tourists in summer, so careful overtaking is wise. Bends are tight in places, with sheer drops on the outer edge, and fog or rain can reduce visibility sharply. In winter, ice and snow close the pass temporarily. Cattle and horses sometimes graze near the road, and wildlife such as marmots and eagles can be seen.

The nearest sizable settlement is Onguday, a village with a few thousand people, a few kilometres from the pass, with shops, cafés and fuel. Another good option for fuel is a bit further on, but it is wise to fill up whenever you pass a station on this road. Onguday also has the nearby Ongudai museum and some Neolithic rock carvings in the region.

In early summer, the hillsides are covered in flowers, and the larches turn gold in early autumn. A morning start gives you quiet roads and the best light on the mountains, and an evening arrival at a roadside cafe for a bowl of hot soup is a good reward.
t.inya altai@50.5,86.6:
Inya is a small village on the Katun river in the Altai Republic, on the Chuya Highway, and it feels like a place that exists mainly for the river. A bridge crosses the Katun here, and the water runs wide and fast beneath it, a milky turquoise that changes shade with the light and the weather. The surrounding hills are steep and covered in larch and pine, and the village has the unhurried look of a place where people are used to travellers stopping briefly and moving on.

The Katun is a young, wild river, fed by glaciers, and it carves a long valley through the mountains of Altai. In the area around Inya, the river meets other rivers coming in from the high ranges, including the Chuya, and the confluences make a landscape of braided channels, gravel bars and clear tributaries. The colour contrast where waters meet, milky and clear, is a visual treat, and you can often see it from the bridge or from viewpoints on the road.

The area has long been inhabited, and archaeologists have found many traces of ancient peoples, with burial mounds, standing stones and rock carvings scattered across the Altai. Local people, Altaians, have traditional beliefs rooted in the mountains and rivers, and you may see small offerings of ribbons or coins at passes and springs. Respect for these places is part of travelling here.

The road from the Chike-Taman Pass to Inya follows the Katun through a series of bends, where the river is often just below the road, with views of cliffs, rapids and forested slopes. The asphalt is generally decent, with occasional patches of rough surface, and traffic includes trucks, buses and the occasional horse. Rafting companies run trips on the Katun in summer, and the sight of colourful boats bouncing through the rapids is a feature of the river.

There is a shop or two and a few cafés in Inya, and fuel may be limited, so it is wise to fill up at the larger villages along the route. The local food includes grilled river fish and meat dumplings, and the tea is served hot and strong. Summers are warm by day and cool at night, with the best months from June to September. Winter closes in with snow and hard frost.
t.kosh agach@50.0,88.7:
Kosh-Agach is the last real town on the Chuya Highway, a windswept settlement on a high steppe in the far southeast of the Altai Republic, close to the borders with Mongolia and Kazakhstan. It sits at about 1,750 metres above sea level on a broad, dry plateau ringed by snow-capped ranges, and everything about it feels remote: the huge sky, the dry grass, the cold air that smells of dust and sage. It is a place where the steppe of Central Asia begins.

The Chuya steppe is one of the coldest and driest places in Siberia. Cold air pools in the basin on winter nights, and temperatures can drop to minus fifty, among the lowest recorded in Russia outside the north-east. In summer the days are bright and warm, but nights are cool, and there is almost always a wind. The surrounding mountains, with their glaciers and bare rock, rise to nearly four thousand metres, and the whole area looks like a geographical stage set.

Most of the people here are Kazakhs, descendants of herders who came from the steppes to the south, and Kosh-Agach has the largest Kazakh community in Russia. You will see yurts at summer pastures, horses and flocks of sheep grazing on the plain, and sometimes the sight of riders on horseback herding livestock. The local people are known for hospitality, and hospitality means tea, bread and mutton.

Not far to the south lies the Ukok Plateau, a high, remote tableland where, in 1993, archaeologists found the frozen burial of a woman of the ancient Pazyryk culture, tattooed and preserved in ice for about two and a half thousand years, who became known as the Siberian Ice Maiden. The area is a protected zone and reaching it requires permits.

The road to Kosh-Agach is a long, open run across the steppe, with the surface in good shape in places and broken in others, and heavy winds that can blow riders sideways. Distances are large and services are few, so plan fuel carefully. Kosh-Agach has a few stations, shops and a handful of simple guesthouses, and it makes sense to fill up whenever you can. Border zone rules apply near the frontier, so carry your documents and check for permits before heading further south.

The best months are June to September, and by October snow can already be falling on the surrounding ranges.
t.ulagan@50.6,88.0:
Ust-Ulagan is a small village in the Altai highlands, scattered along a river in a wide, open valley, and it is the starting point of one of the most beautiful mountain roads in the republic. The surrounding country is a landscape of high, rolling pastures, larch woods and distant snowy ridges, where herders drive sheep and horses over summer grass. It is a place of long views and few buildings, and the air is thin and sharp.

The people here are mostly Altaians, in particular the Telengits, a Turkic people with a tradition of herding and shamanism. You may see small shrines with coloured ribbons tied to trees, and horses grazing freely near the road. The local cuisine is simple and based on meat, dairy products and bread, with strong milk tea and a distilled drink made from fermented milk. Villages are small, and every passing traveller is noticed.

The Ulagan Pass road leads west from here, climbing over the ridge toward the Teletskoye Lake region. It is a mountain road that rises through meadows and then into rocky terrain, with views back over the valley and of the peaks beyond. The surface is a mixture of asphalt and gravel, and the high section can be rough, with potholes, washouts and mud after rain. Snow can linger late in spring and return early in autumn. Cloud and fog can roll in quickly, cutting visibility on the descent.

The nearby Katu-Yaryk pass is a different matter altogether, a notorious track that descends in tight serpentines on a narrow shelf above the Chulyshman valley, with long drops and little room for error. It is a challenging route for experienced riders and drivers and should not be attempted in wet weather or without good preparation. Many locals prefer to avoid it, and it is wise to ask before setting out.

Ust-Ulagan has a few shops, simple guesthouses and cafés, but fuel is limited, so fill up in the larger towns before arriving. Mobile signals are patchy. The best time to ride is July to early September, when the road is dry and the pastures are green. Autumn brings golden larches, and winter closes the high routes with snow.
t.artybash@51.8,87.3:
Artybash is a village at the northern end of Lake Teletskoye, where the lake narrows and drains into the Biya river, and its position gives it one of the best views in the Altai. The lake stretches southward between steep, forested mountains for about eighty kilometres, deep, cold and astonishingly clear. In places it is over three hundred metres deep, and the water is so pure that you can see rocks many metres below the surface. The Altai people call it Altyn-Kol, the golden lake.

More than seventy rivers and streams flow into Teletskoye, and only one flows out, the Biya, which later joins the Katun to form the great Ob. The mountains rising from the water are covered in cedar, fir and birch, and the wall of the valley is cut by waterfalls that tumble straight into the lake. The best known of them, the Korbu, can be reached by boat from Artybash, with a short walk through the forest at the end. The lake is part of the Altai Nature Reserve and the Golden Mountains of Altai World Heritage Site.

Artybash itself is a quiet resort village of wooden houses, small guesthouses and a lakeside promenade. In summer, boats run up the lake, and visitors take excursions to waterfalls and remote beaches. The lakeshore holds small cafés selling smoked fish and berries, and the sunsets are dramatic, with light turning the water to gold. The village is at the head of the lake, so there is no through road down the shore, and the long southern part can only be reached by boat or on foot.

For riders, the road to Artybash follows the Biya river through the foothills, running along gentle curves with views of forest and distant ridges. The surface is generally decent, though it can be rough in places, and there are livestock and wildlife to watch for. In summer, tourist traffic makes the road busier, and weekends can be crowded.

The village has a few shops and small stations, but fuel can be limited, and it is wise to fill up in Gorno-Altaysk or Turochak before arriving. The weather changes quickly, with cold mornings and warm afternoons, and thunderstorms in summer. The best months are June to September, and early autumn brings brilliant colour.
t.belokurikha@52.0,85.0:
Belokurikha is a spa town tucked into the northern foothills of the Altai, in Altai Krai, and it has the sort of relaxed, slightly old-fashioned atmosphere that comes from a century of people arriving to get well. The thermal water here is naturally warm and contains radon, a trace of radioactivity that doctors in the Soviet era believed to be healing, and sanatoria sprang up along the hillsides. About fifteen thousand people live in the town, and in summer many times that number arrive for treatment, rest or just fresh air.

The setting is pretty. Forested hills close in around the town, pine and birch on the slopes, with a small river threading through, and above it all rises Mount Tserkovka, which is reached by a chairlift. In winter the slopes become a modest ski area, and in summer people ride up for the view over the foothills toward the Altai ranges. The air has a resinous smell that comes from the pines, and on warm afternoons the town feels almost Alpine.

The area is also rich in prehistory. Not far to the south, Denisova Cave in the Altai has become one of the most important archaeological sites in the world. A tiny finger bone found there led to the identification of a previously unknown human relative, the Denisovans, who lived in Asia tens of thousands of years ago and interbred with our own ancestors and the Neanderthals. The cave can be visited in summer, and its quiet, dim chambers are an extraordinary place to think about deep time.

For a rider, the roads around Belokurikha are quiet and pleasant, rolling through farmland, forest and low hills with views of the mountains ahead. The surface is generally decent, with some rough patches and frost damage in spring. In summer, the traffic increases on the main road to Gorno-Altaysk, and the Chuya Highway lies beyond. Cattle and horses sometimes graze near the road, and watch for deer at dusk.

The town has fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and plenty of hotels, which makes it a comfortable base. Local honey is excellent, and the area is known for herbal teas and pine nuts. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, with warm days and cooler evenings, while winter brings snow and a modest ski season.
t.biysk@52.5,85.2:
The ride begins in Biysk, a city of just over two hundred thousand on the northern doorstep of the Altai, at the point where the Biya and the Katun rivers join to form the Ob. That fact alone gives the place a certain quiet importance, since the Ob goes on to run for thousands of kilometres across Siberia to the Arctic. Zarya and Pervomayskoye are small settlements just beyond the edge of town.

As a starting point it could hardly be easier. Biysk has everything: fuel, markets, cafes, hotels, mechanics and tyre shops, so fill up, eat well and check the bike before you leave. The city is flat and a little sleepy, with wooden houses mixed in among Soviet blocks, and the main roads are broad. Heading south, you leave the steppe behind and climb gradually toward the first foothills, with the Chuysky Trakt, the famous highway to Mongolia, taking over as your road. Early morning is a lovely time, with mist over the river fields and the first hint of blue mountains ahead.

Biysk dates from 1709, when a wooden fort was founded here by order of Peter the Great as a frontier post against nomadic raiders. It grew into a trading town for Altai goods, honey, grain and furs, and its merchant houses still show some of that prosperity. The Chuysky Trakt began as a caravan track to Mongolia and was upgraded into a modern road in the early twentieth century, and Biysk is the traditional start of that journey. There is a museum in town devoted to local history, and the river embankments make a pleasant evening walk.

The landscape on the way out is gentle at first. Wide fields of wheat, sunflowers and rapeseed, with birch groves between them, give way to the Altai foothills, where pine and larch begin to appear. In July the air smells of hay and warm earth, in late September the birches turn gold, and in winter the road can be very cold and icy.

A practical point: the first stretch is busy with trucks and holiday traffic, so be patient and keep alert. The real riding starts south of Gorno-Altaysk, where the road starts to curl along the Katun. Make sure you leave with a full tank and a warm layer.
t.chemal@51.4,86.0:
Chemal sits on the Katun River in the Altai Republic, a village of about three thousand people spread along the water, with the hills closing in on both sides and the river running milky green through the middle. Elekmonar is the closest neighbour, and the only real choice for supplies is here, which is useful to remember: fill the tank in Chemal or earlier before heading further up the valley.

The riding in this area is among the most pleasant in the Altai. The road follows the Katun upstream, with long open bends and views across the water to forested slopes, and as you continue toward Oroktoy the valley narrows, the surface becomes more patchy and the traffic thins. This is a ride for steady speed and frequent stops, because there is so much to look at. The best seasons are late spring, when the slopes turn green, and September, when larch needles go gold. Midsummer brings tourist traffic, and the afternoons can be hot.

Chemal is famous for a tiny rocky island in the Katun called Patmos, reached by a footbridge that hangs over the water, and for the small church of John the Baptist that stands on it. Pilgrims and tourists walk across, and the view from the island up and down the river is the postcard picture of the region. A hydroelectric station was built on the river here in the mid-twentieth century.

The valley is also a place of old rock art and burial mounds, and the Altai as a whole is a UNESCO listed area for its natural diversity. Nearby, the Katun cuts through limestone and granite, forming rapids and pools, and the forests hold cedar, pine, birch and larch. Maral deer, bears and sables live in the surrounding hills, though you are far more likely to meet a cow standing in the road than anything wild.

Chemal has plenty of guesthouses, cafes selling grilled fish, honey and local herbal tea, and small shops. Prices rise in summer. The area can see rain at short notice, and gravel washes onto the road after heavy storms, so ride with care on the bends beyond the village.
t.seminsky pass@51.0,85.6:
The Seminsky Pass is the first real mountain test on the Chuysky Trakt, the old highway that runs from the Siberian plain into the heart of the Altai and on to Mongolia. It tops out at about 1,717 metres, a height that does not sound dramatic until you remember you started in the lowlands, and it separates the green valley around Shebalino from the long run toward Onguday. Shebalino, the nearest town of any size, lies on the north side, so fuel is there, not on the summit.

The road itself is good tarmac, rebuilt over the years and regularly maintained. Up from Shebalino, it winds through larch and pine forest in a series of long, steady bends, climbing more gently than the name suggests. At the top the trees thin out and the light opens, and on a clear day you can see ridge after ridge of Altai mountains fading into blue. The descent to the south is a little steeper, with sharper bends and faster trucks, so use your brakes with care, especially in wet weather. Fog and rain can roll in with surprising speed here, and in winter the pass is icy.

The Chuysky Trakt has a long history. It began as a trade route between Siberia and Mongolia, used by merchants carrying tea, cloth and furs, and in the 1920s it was rebuilt for motor traffic largely by hand, with picks, shovels and dynamite. Today it is one of the most famous roads in Russia, and National Geographic once named it among the most beautiful in the world. The pass is a point on that long story.

Around the summit, the landscape is typical of the northern Altai: taiga forest, mossy clearings and slopes covered with ferns, and in summer a thick scatter of wildflowers. Bees buzz in the meadows, and roadside stalls sell honey from the surrounding hills, which is worth stopping for. Larch needles turn golden in late September, and the air smells of resin.

Practically, check the weather before crossing, wear a warm layer even in summer, and be careful of loose gravel on the shoulder. There are small cafes on both sides, but nothing on the very top except a view.
t.onguday@50.8,86.1:
Onguday is a long, low village in the valley of the Karakol River, a place of about five thousand people that has served for generations as a stopover on the Chuysky Trakt. It is the largest settlement along the road between Gorno-Altaysk and the high south, which means fuel, shops, cafes and guesthouses are available here, and in the Altai that makes it a place worth remembering.

The valley is broad and open, with the river winding through grassland, and the mountains stand back on both sides, bare on the sunny slopes and darker where larch grows. Riding through feels spacious after the narrower roads of the north. From Onguday the highway continues south over the Chike-Taman Pass, a famous stretch of tight serpentine bends that climbs the slope in a few steep switchbacks, with views back over the valley. It is the kind of ride that makes people grin inside their helmet. North of the village, the road climbs toward the Seminsky Pass, with long gentle bends in good condition. Early mornings and evenings are best, since the light is low and the traffic quieter.

Onguday is a good place to think about the long past of the Altai. The region is full of petroglyphs, standing stones and burial mounds left by nomadic peoples over thousands of years, and the Karakol valley has several sites that archaeologists have studied. Local Altai people, the Altaians, have traditionally been herders, and you will see flocks of sheep and horses on the hillsides. The names of the surrounding places, many of them Turkic, tell their own story of movement along the valley.

The nature here is a mix of steppe and taiga. On the lower slopes you find dry grassland and scrub, on the higher slopes pine and larch, and in the valley bottom willows and poplars along the river. Hawks and eagles are easy to spot, and in summer the air smells of dry grass and warm earth.

Practical advice: fill the tank here, buy food and water, and check the bike, because the road ahead is long and the next serious supplies are in Kosh-Agach far to the south. A warm layer is wise, as temperatures drop fast in the evening, even in July.
t.chuya katun confluence@50.4,86.7:
There is a moment on the Chuysky Trakt where two rivers of different colours meet, and this is it. The Chuya, cold, clear and bluish, flows in from the southeast and joins the Katun, which carries a milky green from glacial silt, and for a short distance the two run side by side before blending.

The road runs along the Chuya's valley, cut into the cliffs above the river, with sheer rock walls on one side and a drop on the other. The tarmac is generally good but narrow in places, with blind bends, and the rock face means you sometimes ride through patches of shade even at midday. There are viewing points where cars and bikes pull over, and it is wise to use them, rather than stopping on a corner. The steep rock faces are home to nesting birds, and the river below is loud with rapids. Spring and early summer bring the highest, muddiest water, while autumn is quieter and the colours of the larch and birch glow on the slopes.

The Chuya valley has been a corridor for thousands of years. Nomads moved through it, caravans carried goods from Mongolia, and rock carvings along the road record herds and hunters from the Bronze Age. When the Chuysky Trakt was built in the twentieth century, workers blasted much of it out of the cliffs, and sections still carry the marks of that work. Rafting groups use the Katun here for its strong rapids, and you will see their buses and rubber boats at launch points on busy days.

The landscape is both wild and open. Steep slopes of grass and rock rise above the road, with patches of larch and pine, and snow peaks glimmer in the distance when the sky is clear. The river's sound follows you, and cold air from the water makes the bends feel cool even on a warm day. Hawks hang in the updraft above the cliffs.

Fuel is not available at the confluence, and Inya has only the basics, so fill your tank in Onguday before heading south. Bring a warm layer, water and snacks, and go slowly, since the road is shared with trucks and livestock.
t.kyzyl chin@50.0,88.3:
Kyzyl-Chin is known as the Mars Valley, and the nickname is not an exaggeration. In the dry southeastern Altai, a few tens of kilometres from Kosh-Agach, the Chuya river has cut through soft clay and sandstone, leaving a maze of orange, red and pale yellow ridges, pinnacles and gullies that look like another planet. Kosh-Agach, with just over five thousand people, is the nearest town, so fuel and food are there, not in the valley.

The ride runs along the Chuysky Trakt and then, for the final stretch, along a track or minor road toward the formations. The highway across the Chuya steppe is long, mostly straight and exposed to wind, with the mountains of the Southern Chuya and North Chuya ranges forming a wall of white on either side. The turn to Kyzyl-Chin is easy to miss, and the last stretch can be gravel or sand, so adventure bikes and slow, careful riding work best. Come in the morning or late afternoon, when low light makes the colours glow, and avoid rain, since the clay turns to slippery paste.

Geologists describe the area as an ancient lake bed, with sediments laid down millions of years ago, later uplifted and eroded by water and wind. The soft layers wear away quickly, which is why the shapes look so sculpted. The name Kyzyl-Chin comes from the Altai language and refers to red, and the colour comes from iron minerals in the clay.

The surrounding steppe is high, dry and cold. Few trees grow, and the vegetation is mostly low grass and thorny shrubs, with marmots and hawks among the wildlife. The wind carries the smell of dust and dry herbs, and the quiet is almost total. The Altai people and Kazakhs who live here keep sheep, horses and yaks, and you may see herders on horseback crossing the plain.

Practical advice is simple. Fill the tank in Kosh-Agach, carry water, wear sunglasses and a warm layer, and do not walk onto fragile formations or climb unstable slopes. Mobile signal is poor, so tell someone where you are going.
t.katu yaryk pass@50.9,88.2:
The Katu-Yaryk Pass is one of those places that has a reputation before you arrive, and the reputation is earned. It lies on the track that links the high Ulagan plateau with the deep valley of the Chulyshman River, descending from the plateau edge to the canyon floor in a series of narrow, steep and exposed switchbacks cut into the rock face. Fuel is not available nearby.

This is a track, not a road. The surface is gravel, rock and dirt, narrow in places, with a sheer drop on the outside of many bends, and there is often no room to pass an oncoming vehicle. It is a serious challenge for an adventure motorcycle, and a very bad idea on a road bike or in rain. Ride it slowly, in dry weather, ideally with a companion, and walk the worst corners first if you have doubts. Many riders choose to ride down and decide there whether to return the same way, since the climb back can be just as demanding. Summer and early autumn are the usable season, and the lower valley can be warm while the plateau stays cool.

The region carries a cultural weight that has nothing to do with engineering. The Chulyshman valley is a remote corner of the Altai, home to small communities of Altai and Telengit people who have traditionally herded and hunted here, and reaching the valley floor was for a long time very difficult. The track itself was built to link the plateau and the valley, and it follows an old path used by shepherds and hunters.

The scenery is the reward. Looking down from the top of the descent, you see the deep green canyon of the Chulyshman, with the Akkurum waterfall area and the great cliff walls beyond, while upstream lie the cold, grassy meadows of the Ulagan plateau. Larch forest covers the slopes, and the air smells of pine and cold water.

Bring spare fuel, water, tools and warm clothes, and tell someone your route. Mobile coverage is poor, and recovery would be slow and expensive. Treat the pass as an adventure, not a race.
t.inya@50.5,86.6:
Inya is a small village on the Chuysky Trakt, the great road that runs from Biysk across the Altai Mountains to the Mongolian border, and it sits right on the banks of the Katun, the turquoise river that drains the glaciers of Mount Belukha. An old suspension bridge spans the river here, swaying slightly in the wind, and walking out onto it with the water rushing milky green below is the classic way to break a ride. The village has about two thousand people and the slow, practical feel of a settlement that lives by the road and the river.

A few kilometres downstream, the Chuya River joins the Katun in a confluence of two different colours of water, the grey-white Chuya meeting the bright Katun and running side by side for a while before mixing. Close by, on a rock face beside the road, are the petroglyphs of Kalbak-Tash, thousands of images carved over millennia, from Stone Age hunters to Turkic warriors, showing deer, ibex, horses and strange figures. It is one of the richest rock art sites in Siberia, and you can walk among them in a few minutes from the road.

The Chuysky Trakt is one of the world's great motorcycling roads, and the section around Inya is among its best. The road follows the Katun through a deep valley, with sweeping bends, rocky cliffs and views of the river at every turn. Further east it climbs toward the high, dry steppe of the Kurai and Chuya basins, with snowy peaks of the North Chuya Range on the horizon. The surface is generally good, but watch for trucks, tourist buses and livestock. Summer is the main season; snow and ice arrive early at altitude.

Inya has a shop, simple cafes and guesthouses, but fuel is a question. Onguday, about forty-seven kilometres back toward Biysk, is the nearest larger village with reliable fuel, and Aktash further east is the other option. Fill up whenever you can along the Trakt. Try the local Altai honey, sold at roadside stalls, and a bowl of hot soup in one of the cafes. Then walk out on the bridge and watch the river; there are few better places to feel the power of the mountains.
t.red@50.4,87.6:
The rock walls here are the colour of rust and dried blood, and the road squeezes between them through a gap barely wider than a truck. The Altai people and Russian travellers alike have called it the Red Gate, Krasnye Vorota, and it is the dramatic entrance to the road climbing from the Chuysky Trakt at Aktash up onto the Ulagan Plateau. The colour comes from iron and from cinnabar, the mercury ore that was mined near Aktash in the Soviet period, and the rocks glow most vividly in the low light of early morning and late afternoon.

Aktash, about ten kilometres away, is a small, somewhat tired settlement that grew up around the mercury mine and the road. Beyond the Red Gate, the landscape changes completely. The road climbs onto a high plateau of larch forest, alpine meadows and lakes, with snowy peaks in the distance and the air growing cooler with every bend. This is the territory of the Telengits, one of the Turkic peoples of the Altai, and you will see their wooden houses, horses and sometimes yurts as you climb.

The riding is the main attraction. The road from Aktash through the Red Gate to Ulagan is narrow, with tight bends and steep sections, and it has been progressively paved, though stretches of gravel, washboard and potholes remain. Beyond Ulagan, the road continues to the Katu-Yaryk pass, where it plunges down into the Chulyshman valley in one of the most famous descents in Russia, a series of steep, loose hairpins carved into the cliff. Check the current state of the road before you go, especially after rain.

Services are limited. Aktash has fuel, a shop or two and simple cafes, and is the last reliable place to fill up before heading up onto the plateau. Ust-Ulagan, about forty kilometres further on, has some services, but beyond that, the Chulyshman valley is remote, with only small villages and guesthouses. Carry extra fuel if you plan to go all the way, along with water and food. Stop just beyond the gate, turn back, and look at the red rocks framing the valley below; it is one of those places that photographs never quite capture.
t.pazyryk@50.7,88.1:
In a high, lonely valley on the Ulagan Plateau, a line of low stone mounds marks one of the great archaeological finds of the twentieth century. Here, around two and a half thousand years ago, a nomadic people of the Scythian world buried their chiefs in log chambers beneath piles of stones. Water seeped into the tombs and froze, and the permafrost preserved what was inside: horses with their saddles and harnesses, felt hangings, clothing, tattooed bodies, and a wool carpet with a pile so fine that it is still the oldest of its kind known. That carpet, the Pazyryk carpet, is now in the Hermitage in St Petersburg.

The mounds were excavated by Soviet archaeologists in 1929 and again around 1950, and the finds transformed our understanding of the ancient steppe peoples, their art, and their connections with Persia and China. Today the site is quiet, with just the low stone heaps, a few signs and the wind blowing across the meadows. It takes imagination to see what lay beneath, but the setting, a broad valley among larch forest and mountains, makes it easy to understand why a people of horsemen would choose it as a place for their dead.

The ride to Pazyryk follows the road from Aktash up onto the Ulagan Plateau, then branches off toward the Katu-Yaryk pass and the Chulyshman valley. The road is narrow, partly paved and partly gravel, with washboard sections, potholes and soft edges. It crosses rolling, open terrain with larch woods, lakes and meadows, and the views stretch to distant snowy peaks. Weather at this altitude can change quickly, with cold rain or even snow possible in summer. Bring warm layers.

Ust-Ulagan, about fifteen kilometres away, has a shop, simple cafes and fuel that may or may not be available, so it is wise to fill up in Aktash before heading up. Beyond Pazyryk, the road continues to the edge of the plateau and the dramatic descent into the Chulyshman valley, which is remote and rough. Walk slowly between the mounds and feel the silence, broken only by the wind and the distant call of a raven; this is one of the most atmospheric places in the Altai.
t.iogach@51.8,87.3:
Lake Teletskoye begins here. At its northern tip the lake narrows and spills out into the Biya River, which flows north to join the Katun and form the Ob, one of the great rivers of Siberia. The village of Iogach stands on one bank of the outflow, Artybash on the other, linked by a bridge, and together they form the main gateway to the lake. The Altai name for Teletskoye is Altyn-Kol, the Golden Lake, and legend says a poor man threw a lump of gold into it rather than let it bring more misery.

The lake is long, narrow and very deep, stretching about eighty kilometres south into the mountains, with steep forested shores that rise straight from the water. The water is clear and cold even in midsummer, and there is no road along most of the shore. Boats carry visitors to waterfalls, cliffs and the remote southern end, where the Chulyshman River flows in. The forests around are dense with Siberian pine, fir and birch, home to bears, maral deer and sable, and much of the eastern shore is protected as part of a nature reserve.

As the finish of a ride along the northern road, Iogach is a fitting end. The approach from Biysk and Turochak follows the Biya valley through forest and farmland, with gentle bends and occasional climbs, and the final stretch brings the first views of the lake opening out ahead. The surface is generally paved but can be rough and potholed, especially near the end. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic and crowds of holidaymakers, so midweek or early autumn are better times to visit.

Iogach and Artybash have plenty of guesthouses, campsites and cafes, and the shops sell smoked fish from the lake, including grayling, which is worth trying. Fuel availability can be limited, so fill up in Turochak, about fifty-four kilometres away, before heading up. Take a boat trip if you have time; the lake is best seen from the water, with the mountains rising on both sides. Then find a quiet spot on the shore and watch the evening light on the water, which turns from blue to silver to gold as the sun goes down.
